instructions.content: If code is hard to test, treat it as a design problem, not a testing problem; fix the coupling rather than compromising the architecture for testability
Test at architectural boundaries, not internal implementation details
Use unit tests for pure business logic, integration tests for boundary adapters, and end-to-end tests for complete user workflows across boundaries
Keep entities as pure functions with no dependencies
Make use cases depend on interfaces (ports), not concrete implementations
Test adapters with fake use cases or real infrastructure
Test infrastructure with integration tests, not unit tests
Step 1: identify hard-to-test code and output a list of testability blockers (blocker, problem, refactor)
Step 2: apply dependency injection so dependencies arrive via constructor or method parameters
Step 3: isolate side effects with the Humble Object pattern, keeping a thin adapter and a pure testable object
Step 4: choose the right test double: stub for queries, mock for commands, fake for a lightweight implementation
Step 5: verify boundary tests with the checklist (entities unit tested, use cases unit tested with mocked ports, adapters and controllers integration tested)
NEVER instantiate concrete dependencies in business logic
NEVER test implementation details
NEVER use real infrastructure in unit tests
NEVER skip tests because code is hard to test; refactor it to be testable
NEVER tangle business logic with infrastructure
NEVER depend on static calls or singletons for behaviour; use injected interfaces and pass instances
NEVER read the current time or random numbers directly in logic; inject a Clock or Random
NEVER leave dependency rules unenforced; verify boundaries with automated architecture tests run in CI
